prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Cities should scrap minimum parking requirements, and they should do it soon.

For most of the last seventy years, American zoning codes have told builders how many parking spaces they must provide, whether or not anyone asked for them. A restaurant must supply a certain number of spaces per hundred square feet, an apartment building a certain number per unit, and a dentist's office a certain number per treatment room. These numbers did not come from careful study of what people need. Many were copied from neighboring towns or drawn from a handbook of suburban sites measured at their busiest hour, and then written into law as though they were physics.

The result is a built environment shaped more by the needs of parked cars than of people. Surface lots surround shops that could have stood side by side, and apartment buildings devote their ground floors to garages instead of storefronts. Walking from one door to the next means crossing an acre of asphalt, which makes walking miserable and driving mandatory, and that in turn seems to justify the next round of parking requirements. It is a loop that a city can break only by changing the rule that started it.

The strongest argument against these mandates is that they hide a cost and hand it to everyone. A single structured parking space can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and an underground space costs even more. Developers do not absorb that money. They pass it on in higher rents and higher prices for goods, so the person who never owns a car still pays for the parking of those who do. Studies of mandated parking have repeatedly found that it raises the cost of housing, and for a family stretching to afford an apartment, a space they neither want nor use is simply a tax.

Mandates also quietly kill projects that would otherwise get built. On a small urban lot, the required spaces can consume so much of the site that a building does not pencil out at all. Old downtown buildings often could not be legally rebuilt under today's codes, because the parking that would be required would not fit on the land. A rule meant to prevent congestion ends up preventing homes, shops, and small businesses in precisely the places best suited to them.

The usual objection is that without requirements, developers will build too little parking and cars will spill onto neighborhood streets. This worry deserves a fair hearing, but it misreads what removal actually means. Repealing a minimum does not ban parking; it lets the builder decide. A developer who needs tenants, or a lender who needs to be repaid, has every reason to provide parking when customers want it. Plenty of suburban projects would still come with generous lots, because the market there demands them. What changes is that a downtown apartment near a train station is no longer forced to build for a level of car ownership that its residents do not have.

Cities that have tried this offer some reassurance. Buffalo eliminated its citywide minimums in 2017, and later studies suggested that developers kept building parking in most cases but tailored it to each project, while some projects that had been stalled finally moved forward. Other cities, from Minneapolis to Edmonton, have since followed, and the sky has not fallen in any of them. If spillover onto the street does become a real problem on a particular block, the better tool is to price the curb sensibly, through permits or metered rates, rather than to force every building to oversupply parking in advance.

There is also a larger principle at stake, which is that land is scarce and valuable, and cities should not dictate its use in such a blunt way. A mandate treats every site as identical and every customer as a driver. A free choice lets a corner café, a senior housing complex, and a big-box store each settle on the amount of parking that suits them. That flexibility matters more as habits change, with more people working from home, using transit, riding bikes, or sharing rides, and a rule written for 1965 cannot anticipate any of it.

Removing minimums is not an attack on drivers. People who drive will still find places to park, and likely at a fairer price, since the cost of a space will no longer be buried in everything else they buy. What they will gain is a city with more homes, livelier streets, and shorter distances between the places they actually want to go. Letting the people who build and pay for a project decide how much parking it needs is a modest idea, and it is long overdue. City councils that care about affordability, climate, and good neighborhoods should repeal their parking minimums this year.
